nutshell: Feature whitening (decorrelating channel features, not just normalizing their mean/variance) improves DNN training but existing methods require expensive per-batch eigendecomposition, extra learnable parameters, and redefining a pretrained model's forward pass. EFW instead folds whitening entirely into the optimizer: it multiplies the weight gradient by a periodically-updated ZCA whitening matrix computed from input-activation statistics, leaving the network's forward/backward pass untouched - so it drops onto SGDM/Adam (as W-SGDM/W-Adam) and works directly on pretrained models.
contributions: Reformulates feature whitening as a pure gradient transformation (right-multiply the weight gradient by a whitening matrix T) instead of a forward-pass module, based on the observation that a pre-whitening layer's 'recovery' transform can be mathematically absorbed into the next layer's weights - so no architecture change, no new parameters, and it works on already-pretrained/well-defined DNNs.

Makes this practical via momentum-averaged activation statistics and infrequent recomputation (statistics every 50 iterations, SVD-based whitening matrix every 500) instead of per-batch eigendecomposition, adding only 10-20% extra memory.

Adaptive, per-layer dampening (scaled by each layer's max singular value) to keep the whitening matrix inversion numerically stable without manual per-layer tuning, plus a gradient-norm-recovery step so an existing optimizer's well-tuned learning rate/weight decay can mostly be reused unchanged.

Validates the resulting W-SGDM/W-Adam optimizers as drop-in replacements across image classification (CIFAR100/10, ImageNet), object detection/segmentation (COCO with Faster/Mask-RCNN and a Swin-T backbone), and person ReID (Market1501, DukeMTMC-ReID).
deficiencies: The paper's own Table 3 undercuts its 'no extra hyperparameter tuning needed' pitch: for ResNet50 on ImageNet, weight decay for W-SGDM/W-Adam is explicitly increased over SGDM/AdamW to get the reported gains, contradicting the same-hyperparameters claim for one of the two headline ImageNet results.

The only comparisons against the directly competing whitening methods (IterNorm, Network Deconvolution) are on small-scale CIFAR100/10 (Table 10) - never on ImageNet, COCO, or ReID - so the central 'EFW is both faster and at least as accurate as prior whitening methods' claim is untested at any scale where the efficiency argument actually matters most.

Outside the CIFAR tables (which report mean±std over 4 runs), ImageNet, COCO, and ReID results are all single-run numbers, so several reported gains (e.g. Market1501 Rank-1 unchanged at 94.5 for R50, or the 0.1-0.7 point margins in Table 6) can't be distinguished from run-to-run noise.

All of EFW's own hyperparameters (momentum α, dampening ε, update intervals T_xx/T_svd) are tuned once on CIFAR100 with ResNet18 (Tables 7-9) and then reused unchanged as defaults for every other dataset, model, and task in the paper, including ImageNet-scale training and a Swin-T transformer - with no check that this single configuration is actually near-optimal outside the setting it was tuned on.
notable: The move that makes the whole method possible is a fairly simple linear-algebra observation: a pre-whitening layer's recovery transform Wr can be folded into the very next layer's weights (W' = W ∘ Wr), so the recovery step and its extra parameters can be dropped entirely once whitening is pre- rather than post-layer - this is what licenses treating whitening as a pure gradient-side operation with zero architectural footprint. Also notable: EFW is applied to Swin-T's self-attention layers in Table 5 and still helps, even though ZCA whitening's channel-correlation motivation was developed for conv/FC layers - the paper reports this as a positive result without examining whether the same theoretical justification actually transfers to attention weight matrices.
